title: 2 Maccabees
subtitle: a Temple defended from heaven, a mother and her seven sons, and the hope of rising again
lead: 2 Maccabees tells again, in Greek and in a very different voice, the story of the Jewish crisis under the Syrian Greek kings, from the last years of Seleucus IV (about 178 BC) to Judas Maccabeus's victory over Nicanor in 161 BC. Two letters from Jerusalem to the Jews of Egypt stand at the head, urging them to keep the new feast of the Temple's purification (1:1–2:18). Then the writer explains that he is boiling down a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene into one book (2:19–32). His story turns on the Temple: Heliodorus is flogged by heavenly riders when he tries to rob it (3), the high priests Jason and Menelaus buy their office and bring in "the Greek way" (4:13), Antiochus IV plunders and defiles it, and the old scribe Eleazar and a mother with her seven sons die rather than eat pork, the sons confessing that God will raise them again (6–7). Judas wins, Antiochus dies in agony (9), the Temple is purified (10:1–8), and the book ends with Judas's dream of the high priest Onias and the prophet Jeremiah praying for the people, the defeat of Nicanor and a new feast on the 13th of Adar (15). It has 15 chapters and 555 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox churches include 2 Maccabees in their Old Testament; Catholics call it deuterocanonical. The Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches read it too; the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches' "Books of Maccabees" (Meqabyan) are other works. Protestants place it among the Apocrypha. It has been at the center of the dispute more than almost any other such book, because Catholic teaching on prayer for the dead cites Judas's offering for the fallen (12:43–45), and because its writer ends by saying of his work, "If it is thin and middling, that was all within my reach" (15:38). It is not in the Jewish Bible. Most scholars read it as a work of Hellenistic Jewish history written in Greek between about 124 BC and the 60s BC, vivid and theological, valuable for the years before the revolt, and less exact than 1 Maccabees on the order of events and the numbers.
facts: The Catholic Church (on the lists of Hippo, Carthage and Florence; defined at Trent, 1546), the Eastern Orthodox churches (the Apostolic Canons and Trullo; named at Jerusalem, 1672; some Orthodox teachers rank it below the Hebrew books), and the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches by long use. Among the Apocrypha for Anglicans and Lutherans (read, not used for doctrine). Not Scripture for the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches (whose Meqabyan are other books), for Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.

An unknown Jewish writer who calls himself the one who "retells" or shortens the history (2:28–31), summarizing the five books of Jason of Cyrene (2:23), a Jew from the Greek city of Cyrene in North Africa, who is otherwise unknown. The two letters at the start (1:1–2:18) come from other hands.

The summary: most scholars, between about 124 BC (the date of the first letter, 1:10) and the 60s BC, when the Romans took Jerusalem; many prefer the late 100s BC. Jason's history was written earlier, at a date no one can fix. The first letter is dated in the year 188 of the Seleucid era (124 BC) and quotes an earlier letter of the year 169 (143 BC; 1:7). The second letter (1:10–2:18) has no date.
Jerusalem and Judea, and the Seleucid court at Antioch, from Seleucus IV (187–175 BC) to the defeat of Nicanor on the 13th of Adar, 161 BC (15:36). It overlaps with 1 Maccabees 1–7.
Unknown: Jerusalem, or a Jewish community of the Greek-speaking world such as Alexandria. The letters are addressed to the Jews of Egypt (1:1, 10).
Greek. Jerome wrote that "the second" book of Maccabees "is Greek, as can be proved from its very style." The first letter may have been translated from Hebrew or Aramaic.

Greek, in Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD) and more than thirty later manuscripts, some with a Lucianic (Antiochene) revision. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus do not have it. The Old Latin, which the Vulgate kept; Syriac, Armenian and Coptic translations.

Hellenistic history in an elevated, emotional style, with a preface and an epilogue by the summarizer (2:19–32; 15:37–39), two festal letters (1:1–2:18), royal and Roman letters (9:19–27; 11:16–38), speeches, prayers (1:24–29; 14:35–36; 15:22–24), martyr stories (6:18–7:42), heavenly appearances (3:24–28; 5:2–4; 10:29–30; 11:8) and the writer's own reflections on God's discipline (5:17–20; 6:12–17).
15 chapters, 555 verses. The Latin Vulgate and many modern Bibles number two places differently: 12:45 here is 12:45–46 there, and 15:37–39 here is 15:38–40.
authorship: Early Christian readers knew the book as the work of an abridger. Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200) calls its writer "the composer of the epitome of the Maccabees" (Doran); "epitome" is the book's own word for its work (2:26, 28). Jerome judged it Greek from its style. Older Catholic writers, such as Florentine Bechtel in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), held that the summarizer is unknown, that Jason probably wrote soon after Nicanor's death in 161 BC, and that the summary cannot be much later than the first letter of 124 BC.

Most scholars agree that the summarizer wrote in good, rhetorical Greek, and that the preface (2:19–32), the epilogue (15:37–39) and probably the reflections on God's discipline (5:17–20; 6:12–17) are his own, while the story comes from Jason. Jason's five books are lost, so how much the summarizer changed cannot be known: as Doran puts it, attempts to reconstruct or date Jason's work are like tilting at windmills. Proposals for the summary's date run from 124 BC (F.-M. Abel, Christian Habicht) through about 124–63 BC (Jan Willem van Henten) to the first century BC or later. Some, like Doran, place the writer in the Greek-speaking Diaspora; others in Jerusalem.

Since Elias Bickerman (1933) most scholars agree that 1:1–2:18 holds two letters: a short one dated 124 BC (1:1–10a, ending with "In the year 188, at Jerusalem") and a longer, undated one from "Those in Judea, with the council of elders and Judas" to Aristobulus and the Jews of Egypt (1:10b–2:18). The common view is that they were first separate works and were joined to the summary later, perhaps when it was sent to Egypt to promote the feast; Arnaldo Momigliano and Habicht proposed that the second was attached to the first, and Jonathan Goldstein made a similar suggestion, and Doran argues for treating each piece on its own. Many doubt that the second letter is a genuine letter of Judas. Bechtel defended both letters.

audience.to: Greek-speaking Jews, above all, as the letters show, the Jews of Egypt (1:1, 10), in the generations after the revolt. They lived among Greeks, read Greek history and rhetoric, and kept their Law in a Greek city. The first letter asks them to keep "the days of the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev" (1:9), the feast of the Temple's purification that we call Hanukkah, and the summary ends with a second new feast, Nicanor's Day (15:36). In its present form, with the letters at its head, the book addresses the Jews of Egypt, to bind Jews far from Jerusalem to its Temple and its feasts; whether the summary itself was written for them is inferred (Momigliano, Doran). Its first known readers were Greek-speaking: the Jewish writer of 4 Maccabees (first century AD) retold its martyrs, and Hebrews 11:35 most likely recalls them, and the church honored Eleazar, the mother and her sons as saints.
audience.why: The summarizer says he wants to give readers enjoyment, an easy way to remember, and benefit (2:25). His story shows the Temple, "whose fame went around the whole world" (2:22), defended by God: when Israel is faithful, Heliodorus is struck down at its door (3); when Israel sins, God lets Antiochus defile it for a time, to correct his people (5:17–20). "Count the punishments as meant, not for ruin, but for the correction of our people" (6:12). The martyrs die for "the laws of our fathers" (7:2) in hope of the resurrection, and their deaths turn God's anger to mercy (7:38; 8:5). Then Judas, helped from heaven, wins back the city and the Temple, and the people decree feasts to remember it. Knowing the readers changes the reading. 2 Maccabees is not a neutral chronicle but a festal and theological history for Jews living among Greeks: it shows that "Judaism" (2:21; 8:1; 14:38), not "the Greek way" (4:13), is the path of honor, that God's Temple is worth dying for, and that the dead who die faithful will live again.
views: Arnaldo Momigliano, Robert Doran and others read the book as written to promote the two new feasts, Hanukkah and Nicanor's Day, among Jews outside Judea; the letters at the head and the decree at the end (10:8; 15:36) frame the whole.

Many scholars, such as Doran and Daniel Schwartz, see the Temple's fate as the book's thread: its sanctity is defended by God when the people are faithful and lost for a while when they sin (3:38–39; 5:17–20). Schwartz stresses that the writer, a Diaspora Jew in his view, thinks of the Jewish people more than of the place.

Jan Willem van Henten reads chapters 6–7 as the heart: the martyrs' deaths turn God's anger and lead to Judas's victories, and 4 Maccabees later builds a whole book on them. For the churches, this is the book's lasting gift: the Catholic lectionary reads chapter 7 on the 32nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C) and in the Common of Martyrs.

For the churches that read it as Scripture, the readers include the church, which hears in it a witness to the resurrection, to faithfulness unto death, and to prayer for the dead. The Orthodox Church keeps the feast of the Holy Maccabean martyrs, Eleazar, the mother and her seven sons, on August 1.

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts 2 Maccabees among the deuterocanonical books, defined as Scripture at Trent (1546), and reads it as inspired witness to the resurrection, to martyrdom, and to prayer for the dead (Catechism 1032).

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern Orthodox churches, and the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches, read 2 Maccabees in their Old Testament from the Septuagint and honor its martyrs as saints on August 1. The Ethiopian Bible's Meqabyan are different works.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place 2 Maccabees among the Apocrypha. Since the Leipzig debate of 1519 they have argued that it cannot establish doctrine, above all prayer for the dead, while many value its martyrs and its history of the years before the revolt.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 2 Maccabees as a Greek summary of Jason of Cyrene's lost history, made between about 124 and 63 BC: a theological, rhetorical history centered on the Temple, best for the years before the revolt, freer than 1 Maccabees with order and numbers.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: 2 Maccabees is not in the Jewish Bible, and there is little sign that the rabbis knew it; but its feasts of Hanukkah and Nicanor's Day were kept, and the Talmud tells its own story of a mother and seven sons who died rather than worship an idol.

sections.b:
Read it as the writer asks: as a summary of a longer history, shaped to give readers "enjoyment," "ease" in remembering, and "benefit" (2:25). The writer says so twice, at the start and at the end, in a voice found elsewhere in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament only in the translator's prologue to Sirach, who also tells of his much sleeplessness (Greek agrypnia, the word of 2:26) and asks readers' pardon where he falls short: he speaks of "sweat and sleepless nights" (2:26), compares himself to a decorator rather than the builder of a house (2:29), and closes by comparing a well-made story to wine mixed with water (15:39). This is a Greek historian's voice.

Then follow the Temple. The book is built around it. The first part shows the Temple safe while Onias is high priest and the Law is kept (3:1); its defender in heaven strikes Heliodorus down (3:39). The second shows it betrayed by its own high priests, Jason and Menelaus (4), and given up for a time to Antiochus because of the people's sins (5:17–20). The third shows the martyrs, whose deaths turn God's anger (6–7), and Judas, who wins it back and purifies it (8:1–10:8). The fourth shows its new enemies, Lysias, Timothy and Nicanor, who threatens to raze it (14:33), defeated in turn (10:9–15:36). Twice the story closes with a feast decreed by the people (10:8; 15:36).

Watch how God acts. Unlike 1 Maccabees, which names God as "Heaven" and tells no miracles, this book speaks of "the Lord," "the Almighty," "the Master," and of "appearances from heaven" (2:21): riders, armies in the sky and angels. It says outright what the suffering means (6:12–17), and it speaks of the resurrection (7:9, 14, 23; 12:43–45; 14:46).

And read it with 1 Maccabees open. The two books tell the same years differently (see "Two books about the same war").

The Plain English is translated for this site from the Greek, as printed by H. B. Swete (1912), who prints Codex Alexandrinus (A), since Codex Vaticanus lacks the books of Maccabees and Codex Sinaiticus lacks this one, and gives the readings of Codex Venetus (V) in his notes. The variant notes report where those manuscripts, the Lucianic text, the Old Latin and the Latin Vulgate differ in ways that matter, as scholars report them; the Göttingen edition by Robert Hanhart (1959) is the standard critical text.

The verse numbers follow Swete and the King James Version. The Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims, and many modern Catholic Bibles, divide two passages differently: the offering for the dead is 12:43–45 here and 12:43–46 there, and the epilogue is 15:37–39 here and 15:38–40 there. The King James Apocrypha and the Douay-Rheims were used only to check the sense. Names use the usual English forms (Judas Maccabeus, Onias, Jason, Menelaus, Heliodorus, Eleazar, Razis, Nicanor, Kislev, Adar), with the Greek in a note where it differs. Dates are kept as the book gives them, in years of the Seleucid era, with the date BC in the notes.

The Temple and its defender. "He who has his home in heaven is himself the overseer and helper of that place" (3:39). The book's heroes are those who defend the Temple and the Law: Onias, Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, Judas. Its villains are those who betray or attack it: Jason, Menelaus, Antiochus, Nicanor, and each meets a fitting end (4:26; 5:9–10; 9:28; 13:8; 15:28–35).

Discipline, not destruction. The writer stops the story to explain that God punishes his own people quickly so as not to wait until their sins are complete, as he does with the nations: "He trains his own people by misfortune, yet he never leaves them" (6:16).

Judaism and the Greek way. The book is the first writing known to use the word "Judaism" (2:21; 8:1; 14:38), and it sets it against "the Greek way" brought in by Jason's gymnasium (4:13). Yet it is itself written in polished Greek and admires Greek virtues, nobility, courage, fame.

Resurrection and the dead. The martyrs die confessing that "the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever" (7:9), and the mother teaches, "Know that God made them, not from things that were" (7:28). Judas makes an offering for soldiers who died with idols' tokens under their tunics, "for he had the resurrection in mind" (12:43). Razis dies calling on God to give his body back to him again (14:46). Onias and Jeremiah, long dead, are seen praying for the people (15:12–14). These passages are why the book matters so much in the debates between churches; the chapter pages show each church's reading.

Help from heaven. Riders and young men in glory strike Heliodorus (3:24–26); armies appear in the sky over Jerusalem (5:2–4); five riders lead the Jews into battle (10:29–30); a rider in white goes before them (11:8); and Judas prays for "a good angel" (15:23).

sections.h: Two books about the same war
sections.b:
2 Maccabees is not a sequel to 1 Maccabees, and it was written separately and in Greek. It covers about 178–161 BC, while 1 Maccabees covers 175–134 BC, so the two overlap in 1 Maccabees 1–7. The 1 Maccabees book page sets out the main differences: the family of Mattathias, the high priests, miracles and angels, the resurrection, the order of events and Hanukkah. In short:

  • The years before the revolt. Only 2 Maccabees tells of Heliodorus (3), of Jason and Menelaus buying the high priesthood (4:7–29), of the murder of Onias (4:30–38) and of Jason's attack on the city (5:5–10). Historians lean on it for these years.
  • The heroes. 2 Maccabees never names Judas's father, Mattathias; Judas withdraws to the mountains "one of about ten" (5:27) and leads alone, while his brothers are minor figures. Its other heroes are the high priest Onias and the martyrs.
  • The order. 2 Maccabees puts the death of Antiochus IV (9) before the purification of the Temple (10:1–8), and Lysias's first campaign (11) after both, under Antiochus V. 1 Maccabees puts Lysias's campaign first (1 Maccabees 4:26–35), then the purification (1 Maccabees 4:36–59), then the king's death (1 Maccabees 6:1–16).
  • The numbers. 2 Maccabees gives larger armies and higher losses: Lysias comes with "about eighty thousand men" and eighty elephants (11:2–4), where 1 Maccabees 4:28 has sixty thousand foot and five thousand horse; Antiochus V and Lysias bring 110,000 foot and 300 chariots (13:2), where 1 Maccabees 6:30 has 100,000 foot and 32 elephants.
  • The feast. 2 Maccabees says the first Hanukkah was kept for eight days "as one keeps the Feast of Booths" (10:6), with palm fronds (10:7), and the letters call it "the days of the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev" (1:9).

Both end their accounts of Judas's great victories with the defeat of Nicanor on the 13th of Adar and a decree to keep the day (15:36; 1 Maccabees 7:43–49). 2 Maccabees stops there, before Judas's death.

In Jewish memory. The feasts the book promotes lived on: Hanukkah, and Nicanor's Day, which the Aramaic Scroll of Fasts (Megillat Ta'anit, first century AD) lists among days when fasting was forbidden. The book itself was not kept; Robert Doran finds very little evidence that Philo, Josephus or the rabbis knew it. The Babylonian Talmud tells a story of its own about a woman and her seven sons, each killed for refusing to bow to an idol; the mother tells the youngest to say to "your father Abraham" that he bound one son on the altar, but she bound seven (Gittin 57b). The story's setting and details differ from 2 Maccabees 7, and it does not cite the book.

In the early church. The mother and her seven sons, with Eleazar, were honored as martyrs, with a feast on August 1. Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom preached on them, and Augustine wrote that the church holds the books of the Maccabees canonical "not by the Jews, but by the Church" because of these martyrs (City of God 18.36). Origen cited the mother's words of 7:28 to show that God made the world from nothing (On First Principles 2.1.5).

In Catholic worship. The Catholic lectionary reads 2 Maccabees 7:1–2, 9–14 on the 32nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C), beside Jesus' answer to the Sadducees about the resurrection; Eleazar (6:18–31) and the mother and sons (7:1, 20–31) on weekdays of the 33rd week (Year I); passages from 6 and 7 in the Common of Martyrs and on the feast of the Ugandan martyrs (June 3); and 12:43–46 (Vulgate numbering) in the Masses for the Dead.

In the Orthodox churches the feast of the Holy Maccabean martyrs, Eleazar, the mother (called Solomonia in the church's tradition) and her seven sons, is kept on August 1.

In the debates of the Reformation no other book outside the Hebrew Bible was argued over so much, because of 12:43–45 (see "Why most churches set it aside" on the canon page).

• Jason of Cyrene, the author of the five-book history this book summarizes (2:23). Not the high priest Jason.
  • Onias III, the godly high priest (3:1), murdered near Antioch (4:34), seen in Judas's dream praying for the people (15:12).
  • Jason and Menelaus, high priests who bought the office from Antiochus IV (4:7–10, 24) and brought in the Greek way.
  • Heliodorus, the minister of Seleucus IV sent to seize the Temple treasury (3:7).
  • Antiochus IV Epiphanes, king 175–164 BC; Antiochus V Eupator, his young son; Lysias, the regent; Demetrius I, who took the throne in 162 BC.
  • Eleazar, the aged scribe (6:18), and the mother and her seven sons (7), the Maccabean martyrs.
  • Razis, an elder of Jerusalem called "father of the Jews" (14:37), who killed himself rather than be taken (14:37–46).
  • Nicanor, the general killed on the 13th of Adar (15:28–36).
  • Judaism and the Greek way (Greek Ioudaismos, Hellēnismos), the book's words for the two ways of life (2:21; 4:13).
  • Appearances (Greek epiphaneiai), God's interventions from heaven (2:21; 3:24; 5:4; 12:22; 14:15); the same root gives the king's title, Epiphanes.
  • Kislev and Adar, the ninth and twelfth months, of the two feasts (10:5; 15:36).

spec.title: Claude's theory: wine and water as the key to the book
spec.body: The epilogue's picture of wine mixed with water (15:39) is usually read as a modest remark about style. My suggestion is that the writer is describing his whole method. His "water" is the plain history he took from Jason, with its dates, letters and campaigns; his "wine" is what he added to make it delight and move: the speeches, the heavenly riders, the martyrs' last words, the reflections on God's discipline. He says at the start that he will leave exactness to the historian (2:28–31) and aim at enjoyment and benefit (2:25), and at the end that a story made only of one or the other does harm. If so, the epilogue is a reading instruction: do not drink the book as pure wine, as if every number and vision were a report, nor as pure water, as if it were only a chronicle. This would fit both the Catholic reading of its admission as being about style and the critical reading of it as rhetorical history.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Jeremiah frames the book
spec.body: The prophet Jeremiah appears only at the book's two ends. In the second letter he hides the tent, the ark and the altar of incense in a cave and says that "The place will stay unknown until God gathers his people in, and mercy comes" (2:7), and the letter ends in the hope that "soon he will show us mercy and bring us together from all that lies under heaven to the holy place" (2:18). In the last chapter Jeremiah appears in Judas's dream as the one "who prays much for the people and the holy city" and gives Judas a golden sword (15:14–16). The letters were probably joined to the summary later, but my suggestion is that whoever joined them saw this frame: the prophet who hid the holy things at the exile now hands Judas the means to keep the city, so that the purified Temple and the new feasts are a first sign of the gathering Jeremiah promised (compare Jeremiah 3:16–18; Jeremiah 31:8–10).

views: Yes. 2 Maccabees is one of the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament. "Two books of Maccabees" are on the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) and of Pope Innocent I (405), and the Council of Florence (1442) named them; the Council of Trent (1546) defined the list, "two of the Maccabees, the first and the second," as sacred and canonical. Augustine wrote that the church holds the books of the Maccabees canonical because of the sufferings of the martyrs they tell. At Leipzig in 1519 Johann Eck, as the record is reported, answered Luther from Augustine that though these books were not in the canon among the Hebrews, the church had received them into the canon. The Catechism cites Judas's offering for the dead (12:45) as Scripture on prayer for the dead (1032).

Yes, in the Old Testament, though Orthodox teachers explain its rank in two ways. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85), which the Council in Trullo (692) received, list "three of the Maccabees," and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named "the Maccabees" among the genuine parts of Scripture; the Orthodox Church in America calls the books of Maccabees "fully part of the Old Testament." Michael Pomazansky, following Athanasius, calls them non-canonical but "useful and instructive." The church keeps the feast of its martyrs on August 1.

Yes for the Coptic church: a Coptic Orthodox diocese's teaching page lists 1 and 2 Maccabees among the deuterocanonical books the Egyptian church received. The book's ancient Syriac and Armenian translations (Doran) show that the Syriac and Armenian churches read it too.
Not this book. The Ethiopian and Eritrean churches count three books of Meqabyan in their Bible, but R. W. Cowley reports that they are not the same as any of the Greek books of Maccabees.

Not Scripture. At Leipzig (1519), when Eck cited it for purgatory, Luther answered, in one English rendering of the record, that the book, "since it is not in the canon, is powerful only for the faithful; against the obstinate it avails nothing," while granting that the church receives it. By 1521 he wrote that it is not among the books of Holy Scripture. His preface (1534) says that it should be thrown out, though "we include it anyway, for the sake of the good story of the seven Maccabean martyrs and their mother." Martin Chemnitz taught that such books may not prove doctrine.

Not canonical, but read. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles names "the Second Book of Maccabees" among the books that, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine."

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon of the Scripture." The Belgic Confession (article 6) lets the church read "the two books of Maccabees" where they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm any point of faith. Calvin said he would not stoop to answer the argument for purgatory from 2 Maccabees, "lest I should seem to include that work among the canonical books," and then argued that Judas is praised only for his hope of the resurrection (Institutes 3.5.8).

No. The Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration. When an inquisitor cited 2 Maccabees 12 for prayers for the dead, the martyr Jacques d'Auchy answered that they are not books "from which a rule or ordinance might be taken."
No. Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) kept the Anglican list of canonical books but dropped the paragraph naming the Apocrypha.
No. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) nearly repeats Westminster: the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture."

traditions.q: The writer ends, "If it is thin and middling, that was all within my reach" (15:38), and calls his work "sweat and sleepless nights" (2:26). Does that admission rule out inspiration? (Whether a book written after prophecy ceased can be Scripture is asked on the 1 Maccabees book page.)
views: Yes, it is evidence against it. Calvin, rejecting the use of 2 Maccabees for purgatory, added that its author himself at the end "asks pardon for any thing less properly expressed," a confession that does not fit the oracles of the Holy Spirit (Institutes 3.5.8). Reformed teachers still make the point: a Westminster church's teaching page reads the closing words as the author admitting his work is only a human attempt.

No. Catholic commentators answer that the apology concerns the style, not the truth: Richard Challoner's note says it "is not said with regard to the truth of the narration, but with regard to the style and manner of writing," and Augustin Calmet that "inspiration did not exclude natural acquirements," comparing Paul, who admits he is no trained speaker (2 Corinthians 11:6). John Henry Newman argued that the writer was inspired without being aware of it: Jason "need not," but the writer of 2 Maccabees "must, have been inspired," and his apology shows only that inspiration need not be felt. The Second Vatican Council teaches that God chose human authors who made full use of their own powers and abilities, so that they are true authors (Dei Verbum 11). Newman compared Luke, who tells of his own careful research (Luke 1:1–4), and the translator's prologue to Sirach, a book in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, whose writer also tells of his long labor and sleepless nights and asks readers to excuse him where he seems to fall short; Newman took both as signs that a writer need not be conscious of inspiration to be inspired.

canon.summary: 2 Maccabees is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox churches, and is read by the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, and some Orthodox teachers rank it below the Hebrew books. It is not in the Ethiopian Bible, whose "Books of Maccabees" are other works. Lutherans and Anglicans place it among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, and it is not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books. Augustine counted the two books of the Maccabees in the canon (On Christian Teaching 2.8.13) and wrote that they are held canonical "not by the Jews, but by the Church," because of the extreme sufferings of certain martyrs who died for God's law before Christ came (City of God 18.36), that is, the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7. The books are on the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) and in Innocent I's letter to Exsuperius (405). The Council of Florence (1442) listed them. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 1546) defined "two of the Maccabees, the first and the second" as sacred and canonical, with an anathema on anyone who does not receive the books entire, and the Catechism (120) lists them. The Catechism cites 12:45 (12:46 in Catholic Bibles) for prayer for the dead (1032). The lectionary reads it on the 32nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C), on weekdays of the 33rd week (Year I), for martyrs and in the Masses for the Dead.

In the Old Testament, read in the Greek of the Septuagint, with 1 and 3 Maccabees (and 4 Maccabees in an appendix in Greek Bibles). The Apostolic Canons (canon 85, late 300s), received by the Council in Trullo (692), list "three of the Maccabees"; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), answering Protestant ideas, named "the Maccabees" among the genuine parts of Scripture. The Orthodox Church in America's answer calls these books "fully part of the Old Testament," while Athanasius's list (367) leaves them out and Michael Pomazansky counts them among the non-canonical books, "useful and instructive"; Kallistos Ware reports that most Orthodox scholars give these books a lower footing. The church honors the martyrs of 6:18–7:42, Eleazar, the mother and her seven sons, on August 1.

In the Coptic church's Old Testament: a Coptic Orthodox diocese's teaching page lists 1 and 2 Maccabees among the deuterocanonical books the Egyptian church received. Doran lists ancient Syriac, Armenian and Coptic translations, which show that these churches read it. These churches never held a council like Trent to define the list.

Not this book. Their 81-book Bible has three books of Meqabyan, but Cowley reports that they are "not the same as any of the 4 LXX books of Maccabees."

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles names "the Second Book of Maccabees" among the other books that, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The King James Version (1611) printed it as the last book of the Apocrypha.

Among the Apocrypha, and ranked low among them. At the Leipzig debate (1519) Luther, answering Eck's appeal to the book for purgatory, said that it is not in the canon and binds only the faithful, while granting that the church receives it. His Defense and Explanation of All the Articles (1521) says it "is not among the books of Holy Scripture" and is not found in Hebrew. His preface to it (1534) says the title cannot be true, that the book should be thrown out, and that "we include it anyway, for the sake of the good story of the seven Maccabean martyrs and their mother," leaving the rest to the reader's judgment. Lutheran confessions never fixed a canon; Martin Chemnitz taught that such books may not prove doctrine.

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 6) names "the two books of Maccabees" among the books the church may read for instruction where they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm faith. The Westminster Confession (1646, 1.3) says the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon of the Scripture" and are to be used only as other human writings. Calvin said he would not stoop to answer the argument for purgatory from 2 Maccabees, "lest I should seem to include that work among the canonical books," and then argued that Judas is praised only for his hope of the resurrection (Institutes 3.5.8).

Not Scripture. The Global Anabaptist Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration. When an inquisitor cited 2 Maccabees 12:43 for prayers for the dead, the martyr Jacques d'Auchy valued the Apocrypha as edifying but said they are not books "from which a rule or ordinance might be taken."
Not Scripture. Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) took over the Anglican list of canonical books but dropped the paragraph naming the Apocrypha.
Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) calls the Apocrypha "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Most evangelical churches hold the 66 books.

Not Scripture. 2 Maccabees is not in the Hebrew Bible, was written in Greek, and left little trace in Jewish writing: Robert Doran finds very little evidence that Philo, Josephus or the rabbis knew it. Josephus told these years from 1 Maccabees, not from this book. Its feasts were kept: Nicanor's Day is in the Scroll of Fasts (Megillat Ta'anit), and Hanukkah is kept to this day, though the rabbis explained it by the miracle of the oil. The Talmud's story of a mother and her seven sons (Gittin 57b) is the same kind of martyr story, told independently. 4 Maccabees, a Jewish work in Greek of the first century AD, retells the martyrdoms of 2 Maccabees 6–7 as a lesson in reason ruling the passions.

Read and valued from the beginning, above all for its martyrs. Hebrews 11:35 most likely recalls them (see "Where the Bible refers to it"). Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200) knew "the epitome of the Maccabees," and Origen cited the mother's words of 7:28 "in the book of Maccabees" (On First Principles 2.1.5). Augustine counted it in the canon and explained that the church holds it for the sake of its martyrs; he also wrote, against those who cited Razis to justify suicide, that the book narrates Razis's deed without praising it (Letter 204). Writers who followed the Hebrew count placed it lower: Jerome said the church reads the books of the Maccabees but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, and judged the second book to be Greek; Athanasius and Cyril of Jerusalem left them out; Rufinus counted them among the "ecclesiastical" books. The Apostolic Canons listed three books of Maccabees, and the North African councils and Innocent I two.

provenance.h: A summary of Jason of Cyrene
provenance.b: The book says plainly what it is. After the letters, a new voice begins: "Jason of Cyrene told all this in five books, and we will try to boil it down into one" (2:23). The writer explains his aims (2:24–25), his labor (2:26–27), and the difference between the historian, who must "go into the matter deeply" and "busy oneself with every detail," and the one who retells it, who aims at "a short telling" (2:30–31). At the end he speaks again, in the first person, about how well he has done (15:37–39). Nothing else is known of Jason, a Jew from Cyrene in North Africa, a city with a large Jewish community (compare Acts 2:10; Acts 11:20). His five books are lost, so no one can say how much of the present book is his and how much the summarizer's. Most scholars think the preface and epilogue, and the reflections on God's purpose in the suffering (5:17–20; 6:12–17), are the summarizer's own.

provenance.h: When and where it was written
provenance.b: The story ends in 161 BC with Nicanor's defeat, "From those times on the Hebrews held the city" (15:37), which suggests the writer wrote before the Romans took Jerusalem in 63 BC, or at least ignored that event. The first letter, which now stands at the head of the book, is dated in the year 188 of the Seleucid era, 124 BC (1:10). Scholars who think the summarizer himself placed the letters there date the book soon after 124 BC (F.-M. Abel, Christian Habicht); others think the letters were added later and date the summary anywhere from the late 100s to the first century BC; Jan Willem van Henten proposes 124–63 BC. Bechtel, writing for the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), thought Jason finished soon after 161 BC and the summary cannot be "very much later" than 124 BC. Where it was written is also debated: the letters are addressed to Egypt, the Greek is polished, and Doran and Schwartz place the writer in the Diaspora, while others think of Jerusalem.

provenance.h: The two letters at the head
provenance.b:
The first letter (1:1–10a), from "the Jews in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea" to "the Jews in Egypt" (1:1), urges them to "keep the days of the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev" (1:9). It recalls an earlier letter of the year 169 (143 BC), written in the trouble that came "after Jason and his people broke away from the holy land and the kingdom" (1:7). It ends "In the year 188, at Jerusalem" (1:10), 124 BC. Many scholars accept it as a genuine letter, perhaps translated from Hebrew or Aramaic.

The second letter (1:10b–2:18), from "Those in Judea, with the council of elders and Judas" to Aristobulus, "the teacher of King Ptolemy," and the Jews of Egypt, has no date. It tells of the death of Antiochus in the temple of Nanea in Persia (1:13–16), of the sacred fire that Nehemiah found as "thick water" and that blazed up on the altar (1:18–36), and of Jeremiah hiding the tent, the ark and the altar of incense (2:1–8). Most scholars doubt that it is a real letter of Judas; Bechtel defended it as written about 163 BC from early, distorted news of the king's death. How the punctuation is read matters here: older readers, following the King James Version, put the date "in the year 188" at the head of the second letter, which made Judas, who died in the year 152, write a letter thirty-six years after his death, as the Reformed writer Archibald Alexander objected in 1826. Modern editions end the first letter with that date.

Unlike 1 Maccabees, this book was written in Greek, in a style full of the devices of Greek rhetoric: wordplay, long periodic sentences, rare and poetic words, and strong emotion. Jerome noticed it: in his preface to Samuel and Kings (about 391) he wrote that he found the first book of Maccabees in Hebrew, but "the second is Greek, as can be proved from its very style." Florentine Bechtel likewise notes that Greek idioms and constructions are very numerous and Hebraisms few. The New American Bible's introduction ties the book's Greek to its exclusion from the Hebrew canon. The writer knows Greek historians' habits: he speaks of his readers' pleasure, compares his work to painting a house and to mixing wine (2:29; 15:39), and uses Greek moral words such as nobility (6:28, 31; 14:42).

The Greek survives in Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD) and in more than thirty later manuscripts, some of which carry the Lucianic (Antiochene) revision. Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) has 1 and 4 Maccabees but not this book, and Codex Vaticanus (B) has no books of Maccabees. Robert Hanhart's Göttingen edition (1959) is the standard critical text. Swete's edition, used for this site, prints Alexandrinus with Venetus in its notes. The two codices differ in many small ways; in one place, the date at 1:10, Alexandrinus reads only "the eighty-eighth year" and Venetus adds "hundred."

The Old Latin was made from the Greek in the early centuries and survives in several forms. Jerome did not translate the books of Maccabees, so the Latin Vulgate kept the Old Latin. That Latin was the Catholic 2 Maccabees for more than a thousand years, and the Douay-Rheims translated it. It differs from the Greek in some places that matter: at 12:43 the Vulgate has Judas send "twelve thousand" drachmas, where the Greek has two thousand, "for sacrifice to be offered for the sins of the dead"; and it divides 12:45 and the epilogue differently, so that its 12:46 reads, in the Douay-Rheims, "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins," the sentence that was quoted at Leipzig in 1519 and stands in many Catholic Bibles. There are also Syriac, Armenian and Coptic translations (Doran).

provenance.h: How Jews and Christians first used it
provenance.b: The book's martyrs had the widest life. Hebrews 11:35–36 most likely recalls them. The Jewish work 4 Maccabees, in Greek, retells the deaths of Eleazar, the mother and her sons at length. Christians honored them as saints: Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom preached on them, and Augustine, preaching on their feast, mentions their church at Antioch (Sermon 300). Clement of Alexandria knew the book as "the epitome," and Origen quoted 7:28 to show that God made the world from nothing. Augustine both counted the book in the canon and read it critically: Razis, he said, was "not wise in choosing death, but impatient in bearing humiliation," and the book reports his deed rather than praising it (Letter 204.7). Among Jews the book itself left little trace, but its feasts were kept, and the Talmud tells its own story of a mother and seven sons (Gittin 57b).

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
2 Maccabees draws on the Hebrew Bible throughout, and these links run from the Hebrew Bible to 2 Maccabees, not the other way.

  • The Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32): the seven brothers quote "And he will show his servants pity" (7:6; Deuteronomy 32:36), a song about God punishing and then pitying his people, the book's own pattern.
  • Hezekiah and Sennacherib (2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36): Judas recalls the 185,000 struck down and prays for "a good angel" (8:19; 15:22–23).
  • Daniel 11–12: the same crisis, and the first clear promise that many who sleep in the dust will awake (Daniel 12:2), which the martyrs' confession of the resurrection (7:9, 14) builds on.
  • Jeremiah: the prophet of the exile, who hides the holy things (2:1–8) and prays for his people (15:14), a role that goes beyond the book of Jeremiah, which says the ark will not be remembered or made again (Jeremiah 3:16).
  • Fire from heaven: Moses' and Solomon's sacrifices consumed by fire (2:10; Leviticus 9:24; 2 Chronicles 7:1), and Nehemiah's fire (1:18–36), a story not in the book of Nehemiah.
  • Nehemiah's library: "He collected the books about the kings and prophets, and David's books" (2:13), an early report of a collection of sacred books, often cited in the history of the canon.
  • Mordecai's day: Nicanor's Day falls on the 13th of Adar, "one day before Mordecai's Day" (15:36), the earliest outside mention of Purim (Esther 9:17–21).

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible has 24 books (the Protestant Old Testament's 39 counted differently), and 2 Maccabees is not among them. Josephus, about AD 95, says the Jews have 22 books, written from Moses to Artaxerxes, and that later history is not trusted equally "because of the failure of the exact succession of the prophets" (Against Apion 1.41). 2 Maccabees was written centuries later, in Greek, outside that line. Protestants argue, in their strongest form, that the Old Testament was entrusted to Israel (Romans 3:2), that Jesus and the apostles used Israel's Scriptures, and that the church should receive the books Israel received. Whether a book written after prophecy ceased can be Scripture is argued in full on the 1 Maccabees book page.

Jerome (about 347–420), who made his Old Testament from the Hebrew, wrote that what is outside the Hebrew books is to be set among the apocrypha, that the second book of Maccabees is Greek by its very style, and that the church reads "the books of the Maccabees" but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, reading them for building up the people, not to confirm church doctrine. Article VI of the Church of England quotes him ("as Hierome saith"). Athanasius (367) and Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) left the Maccabees out of their lists, and Rufinus counted them among the "ecclesiastical" books. Augustine and the North African councils, by contrast, counted two books of Maccabees in the canon.

The book itself says that it is a human summary of a human history: "we will try to boil it down into one" (2:23); the work cost "sweat and sleepless nights" (2:26); exactness is left to the historian (2:28). And it ends: "If it is well written, and its arrangement hits the mark, that is what I myself was hoping for. If it is thin and middling, that was all within my reach" (15:38). Protestant writers since Calvin have read this, in its strongest form, as the book's own disclaimer. A prophet speaks the word of the LORD and does not ask readers to excuse him; this writer hopes he has pleased them. Calvin wrote that the author "asks pardon for any thing less properly expressed," which no one would say of the oracles of the Holy Spirit (Institutes 3.5.8). The argument is not unanswered: the translator's prologue to Sirach, in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, also speaks of labor and sleeplessness and asks readers' pardon, and Catholic writers take the two together. The question is the second card under "Where Christians differ" on the book page.

rejected_why.h: Prayer for the dead, Leipzig 1519 and the Reformers
rejected_why.b: No other passage outside the Hebrew Bible did as much to shape the Protestant view of these books as Judas's offering for the dead (12:43–45). At the Leipzig debate in July 1519, Johann Eck cited it for purgatory, by the reported accounts in the Vulgate's words, "It is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead." Luther, who still held then that purgatory exists, admitted the text but answered, in one English rendering of the record, that the book, "since it is not in the canon, is powerful only for the faithful; against the obstinate it avails nothing," and appealed to Jerome. He also granted, "I know the Church receives this book," distinguishing "'canon' in one sense and 'canon' in another." Eck replied, from Augustine, that the church had received these books into the canon, by one report adding that they were not in the canon among the Hebrews. The exchange turned a question about one doctrine into a question about the canon. By 1521 Luther wrote that the book "is not among the books of Holy Scripture"; his preface of 1534 said it should be thrown out. Calvin said he would not stoop to answer it, "lest I should seem to include that work among the canonical books," and then answered it anyway: "We may add, that the piety of Judas is commended for no other reason than for having a firm hope of the final resurrection" (Institutes 3.5.8). The Council of Trent then defined the canon with both books of Maccabees (1546); the Thirty-Nine Articles named the Second Book of Maccabees among the books read but not used "to establish any doctrine" (1563, 1571); and the Westminster Confession (1646) called the Apocrypha "no part of the canon." The Protestant argument, in its strongest form, is that a doctrine not taught in the books all agree on cannot rest on one disputed book, and that the passage itself sits uneasily with Hebrews 9:27 and with the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ (Hebrews 10:12–14). Whether sins can be cleansed after death is asked on the chapter 12 page, in the card "Judas had atonement made for the dead, 'to free them from the sin' (12:45). Can sins be cleansed after death, as the Catholic teaching on purgatory holds? (For the wider question whether the living may pray for the departed, see the card at Psalm 130.)"

Protestant writers also point to the ways 2 Maccabees disagrees with 1 Maccabees, which most of them valued as history. It tells the death of Antiochus IV twice, and differently from 1 Maccabees: stoned and cut to pieces by the priests of Nanea in a temple in Persia (1:13–16); struck with a disease of the bowels, eaten by worms and dying in the mountains (9:5–28); while 1 Maccabees has him fall sick from grief and die (1 Maccabees 6:8–16). It puts his death before the Temple's purification, and Lysias's first campaign after it (9–11), the reverse of 1 Maccabees. Its armies and losses are larger (11:2–4; 12:20; 13:2). It is full of heavenly riders and angels, while 1 Maccabees tells of no heavenly appearances (it only recalls the angel who struck Sennacherib's army, 1 Maccabees 7:41). Archibald Alexander (1826) added the fable-like story of the fire hidden in a pit (1:19–22) and the letter that seemed to have Judas writing in the year 188. On this view a book whose history is so often out of line with the better source cannot be the Word of God, however edifying its martyrs.

The book praises Razis, an elder of Jerusalem who, when Nicanor's soldiers came for him, "turned his sword on himself," threw himself from the wall, and tore out his entrails and hurled them at the crowd (14:41–46): "He wanted a noble death sooner than to become the prisoner of villains" (14:42). Archibald Alexander wrote that Razis "is spoken of with high commendation, for destroying his own life," and that "suicide is not, in any case, agreeable to the word of God." Protestant writers also object that the book makes Judas offer a sin offering for men who died in idolatry (12:40–45), which Calvin put down to misguided zeal (Institutes 3.5.8), and that it teaches that the martyrs' deaths turn God's anger from the nation (7:37–38). The notes on 14:37–46 and the chapter pages give the readings of each church.

On the canon. The Catholic answer rests on the councils: Hippo, Carthage, Innocent I, Florence and Trent received these books, so the canon was the church's to recognize, not the rabbis'. Augustine already wrote that the church held these books canonical for the sake of the martyrs, and Eck at Leipzig answered Luther the same way.

On the writer's apology. Catholic commentators say it concerns style, not truth (Challoner), that inspiration did not exclude natural gifts (Calmet), and that a writer may be inspired without being aware of it (Newman, who sets the epilogue beside the translator's prologue to Sirach, where the writer too asks pardon for his shortcomings); Dei Verbum 11 teaches that the human writers were true authors who used their own powers. See the second card.

On the differences from 1 Maccabees. Bechtel argued that the accounts of Antiochus's death "fit very well into one another" once the second letter is read as reporting early, distorted news, that the book counts its years from autumn and so dates some events a year later, and that the campaign of chapter 11 "is not the same" as that of 1 Maccabees 4. Catholic teaching on literary forms (Divino Afflante Spiritu; Dei Verbum 12) asks what each writer meant to assert, and the New American Bible's introduction, published by the Holy See, says openly that the writer rearranges events, exaggerates numbers and composes speeches.

On Razis. Augustine answered that the book reports Razis's deed without praising it, and that he "was not wise in choosing death, but impatient in bearing humiliation" (Letter 204.7). Catholic teaching holds suicide gravely contrary to the love of self, neighbor and God (Catechism 2280–2283).

On prayer for the dead. The church reads 12:43–45 as witness to a practice already in Israel before Christ, and grounds its teaching on purification after death in the church's tradition as well (Catechism 1031–1032).

Orthodox teachers do not appeal to Florence or Trent. They point to the Septuagint the church has always read, to the Apostolic Canons (canon 85), received at Trullo (692), and to the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), which named "the Maccabees" among the genuine parts of Scripture against the Calvinist confession of Cyril Lucaris. Their strongest witness is their worship: the Maccabean martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7 are honored as saints on August 1. At the same time the Orthodox are open about their division over the rank of these books: Pomazansky, following Athanasius, calls them "useful and instructive" but not canonical, while the Orthodox Church in America calls them "fully part of the Old Testament." The Orthodox pray for the dead, and their teachers generally reject purgatory as the Latin church defined it; yet the same Confession of Dositheus (decree 18) says that some souls who repented before death "depart into Hades, and there endure the punishment due to the sins they have committed," and are delivered "through the prayers of the Priests, and the good works which the relatives of each do for their Departed," above all the bloodless sacrifice. Catholic writers point to this; Orthodox writers read it as other than purgatory. That question belongs to the chapter 12 page.

cited_in.b: The strongest link between 2 Maccabees and the New Testament. Hebrews tells of women who received their dead raised to life, of others who were tortured and turned down release to win a better resurrection, and of others who were mocked and whipped, chained and imprisoned (Hebrews 11:35–36). The word for "tortured" (Greek etympanisthēsan, from tympanon) is the word for the instrument Eleazar walked toward, the "torture frame" (6:19, 28). The seven brothers refuse the king's offers and die in hope that God "will raise us again" (7:14), "to live again forever" (7:9), while the king will have "no resurrection to life" (7:14): a better resurrection than the return to this life of the women in 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 4. And the second brother is led out "for their cruel game" (Greek empaigmos, 7:7; compare 7:10), and the brothers are whipped (7:1). Commentators of every tradition draw the link: Moulton in Ellicott's commentary points to the aged Eleazar and the seven brethren, the Cambridge Bible to 6:18–30 and 7:1–10, Vincent to 6:19, 28 and 7:9, 14, and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown to the fourth brother's words about resurrection. Doran too says the martyrs are mentioned probably here. Hebrews goes on to those who wandered in deserts and mountains and hid in caves and holes in the ground (Hebrews 11:38), and the Cambridge Bible on that verse cites Judas, who "lived like the wild beasts in the mountains" (5:27), those who "had gathered in caves nearby to keep the seventh day in secret" (6:11), and the people who had been "living like wild animals in the mountains and the caves" (10:6); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown cite 5:27. Hebrews names no book, and the stories were also told elsewhere (4 Maccabees), so the link is to these martyrs, most likely as 2 Maccabees told them. Catholic and Orthodox writers see it as the New Testament honoring the book; Protestant writers answer that Hebrews also mentions events from outside Scripture, and that an allusion does not make a book canonical (compare Jude 14–15 and 1 Enoch).

Paul speaks of his former way of life "in Judaism" (Galatians 1:13–14), the only use of the word Ioudaismos in the 66 books. 2 Maccabees is the first book known to use it: the brave men who fought "for Judaism" (2:21), those "who had held on to Judaism" (8:1), and Razis, who "had staked body and soul on Judaism" (14:38). Meyer and Vincent on Galatians 1:13 cite these verses. A shared word, not a quotation; Paul does not cite the book.

Gamaliel warns the council that if the apostles' work is from God, they may be found "fighters against God" (Acts 5:39, Greek theomachoi). The sixth brother tells Antiochus that he will not go free "after you have set out to fight against God" (7:19, Greek theomachein). The Expositor's Greek Testament on Acts 5:39 cites 7:19. A shared word for opposing God, not a quotation.

Hebrews says that by faith we understand that the ages were put in order by God's word, so that what is seen did not come into being from things that appear (Hebrews 11:3). The mother tells her youngest son to look at the sky and the earth and "Know that God made them, not from things that were" (7:28), the earliest Jewish saying often read as creation from nothing (whether it means that is asked on the chapter 7 page). The Cambridge Bible on Hebrews 11:3 quotes 7:28 in the Greek order ex ouk ontōn. Origen later cited 7:28 for the same teaching. A shared belief, not a quotation; scholars debate whether 7:28 means "from nothing" in the later sense.

"The Festival of Dedication came around in Jerusalem. It was wintertime" (John 10:22). 2 Maccabees tells how the Temple was purified on "the twenty-fifth of the same month, Kislev" (10:5), and how the people decreed "these days were to be kept every year" (10:8), and its letters urge the Jews of Egypt to keep "the days of the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev" (1:9; compare 1:18). Commentators on John, such as the Cambridge Bible, cite 10:1–8 with 1 Maccabees 4 for the feast's origin. John names the feast, not the book.

When Jesus asks who people say he is, some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, "Still others say Jeremiah, or one of the prophets" (Matthew 16:14). Only Matthew names Jeremiah. Ellicott's commentary explains the name from the traditions in 2 Maccabees: Jeremiah hid the tent, the ark and the altar until God would gather his people (2:1–8), and in Judas's dream he is the one "who prays much for the people and the holy city" (15:14). So some Jews expected Jeremiah to return or to act for Israel. A shared tradition, not a quotation.

Herod Agrippa I, who let the crowd hail him as a god, was struck by an angel of the Lord and "eaten by worms" (Acts 12:23). 2 Maccabees tells of Antiochus IV, who thought he could command the sea and touch the stars: "Worms came boiling up out of the impious man's body" (9:9). The Cambridge Bible and Vincent on Acts 12:23 both compare 9:9. The death of a proud persecutor by worms was a known pattern; Acts does not cite the book.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish faith in the century before Jesus, 2 Maccabees is of the first importance: it gives some of the earliest and clearest Jewish statements of bodily resurrection for the faithful, of martyrdom for the Law, of prayer and offering for the dead, of the dead saints praying for the living, and a saying often read as creation from nothing (7:28; whether it means that is asked on the chapter 7 page), and it is the first book to name "Judaism." As a text, it is fairly well preserved in Greek, its original language, though in only one of the great early codices (Alexandrinus) and in the eighth-century Venetus. As history, it is mixed: very valuable for the years before the revolt, which only it describes, with documents most historians accept; weaker on the order of events after 164 BC, on numbers and on Antiochus's death, which it tells in two ways; and openly theological, with heavenly appearances and composed speeches. Its own writer says he left exactness to his source. The churches that hold it as Scripture read it as true history told in a rhetorical form; Protestant churches mostly value its martyrs and its early history while denying it the authority of Scripture. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with their faith in the one Creator and the hope of resurrection, goes beyond them on prayer for the dead and the intercession of the departed, and in a few places, such as its praise of Razis, may conflict with them.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish faith before Jesus: very high
sections.b: Here no church disagrees. 2 Maccabees shows what many Greek-speaking Jews believed in the 100s BC: that God will raise the faithful dead bodily, "to live again forever" (7:9; 7:11, 14, 23, 29; 14:46), while for the persecutor "there will be no resurrection to life" (7:14); that God made the world "not from things that were" (7:28), often read as creation from nothing (whether it means that is asked on the chapter 7 page); that God disciplines his people to correct them (6:12–16; 7:32–33); that the deaths of the righteous can turn God's anger (7:37–38); that one can pray and offer sacrifice for the dead (12:42–45); that the righteous dead, Onias and Jeremiah, pray for the people (15:12–14); that angels defend God's people (3:24–26; 10:29–30; 11:6–8; 15:23); that the Temple's holiness serves the people: "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (5:19); and that the Sabbath and food laws are worth dying for (6:6–11, 18–31). It gives, with 1 Maccabees 4 and 7, the oldest account of the feasts of Hanukkah (10:5–8) and Nicanor (15:36), and the earliest outside mention of Purim (15:36). Much of this belief stands behind the New Testament: the Sadducees' question about the resurrection (Mark 12:18–27), the hope of Martha (John 11:24) and the roll of the martyrs in Hebrews 11.

Fairly well. Unlike 1 Maccabees, Judith or Tobit, 2 Maccabees was written in Greek, so the Greek is the original, not a translation. It survives in Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD) and Codex Venetus (700s AD) and some thirty later manuscripts, with a Lucianic revision and the Old Latin, Syriac, Armenian and Coptic versions as further witnesses; it is missing from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The witnesses differ mostly in small things, word order, spelling and a word here and there, but some differences matter, such as the numbers (the Vulgate's "twelve thousand" drachmas at 12:43 against the Greek's two thousand) and the punctuation of the letters (whether "the year 188" ends the first letter or begins the second, 1:10). No copy was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Josephus did not use the book, so there is no early paraphrase to check it against, except 4 Maccabees (first century AD) for the martyr chapters (6:18–7:42).

Where it is strong. For the years before the revolt, 175–167 BC, 2 Maccabees is the main source, and historians use it with confidence: the sale of the high priesthood to Jason and then Menelaus, the gymnasium in Jerusalem (4:7–15), the murder of Onias near Daphne (4:33–34), Jason's attack (5:5–10). Its royal officials and their titles fit what is known of the Seleucid court; an inscription found at Maresha in Israel and published in 2007 shows that in 178 BC Seleucus IV, writing through his minister Heliodorus, probably the man of chapter 3, put the temples of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia under a royal overseer, Olympiodoros, which fits the background of chapter 3. Most historians accept the four letters of chapter 11 (11:16–38) as genuine documents, even if they doubt their order.

The three deaths of Antiochus. The book tells the king's death twice. The second letter has him killed with his men by the priests of the temple of Nanea in Persia, struck with stones from a hidden door in the ceiling and cut to pieces (1:13–16). The summary has him driven back from Persepolis, struck by God with pain in his bowels, thrown from his chariot, eaten by worms, repentant too late, and dying "in a foreign land, among the mountains" (9:1–28). 1 Maccabees has him fail to plunder a temple in Elymais and die of sickness and grief in the year 149 (1 Maccabees 6:1–16). The Greek historian Polybius says that Antiochus, wanting money, set out against the sanctuary of Artemis in Elymais, failed, and on his retreat "died at Tabae in Persia, smitten with madness, as some people say" (Histories 31.9), and Josephus, who follows 1 Maccabees, quotes Polybius and argues that the king died for plundering the Temple in Jerusalem (Antiquities 12.354–359). A Babylonian king list records that his death was heard of in Kislev of the year 148. The accounts agree on a failed temple robbery in the east and a death on the way; they differ on how he died. Many scholars think the second letter repeats an early rumor, perhaps confused with the death of his father Antiochus III, who was killed robbing a temple of Bel in Elymais in 187 BC, and that chapter 9 is shaped by the pattern of the proud tyrant's death (compare Isaiah 14:12–15). Bechtel argued that the accounts fit together.

The letters of chapter 11. The four letters are dated in the year 148: Lysias's letter "on the twenty-fourth of Dioscorinthius" (11:21), a month not otherwise known; the king's letter to the Jews and the Roman envoys' letter both "on the fifteenth of Xanthicus" (11:33, 38); and the king's letter to Lysias, which says "Our father has gone over to the gods" (11:23), is undated. The book places them all after the death of Antiochus IV, under his son. Many historians think the letter of 11:27–33 is a genuine letter of Antiochus IV himself, written before his death and before the Temple's purification. Its own date, the fifteenth of Xanthicus in the year 148 (11:33), would fall about March 164 BC; Doran thinks that date unlikely and places the letter in early 165 BC. Many also think that 11:22–26 is Antiochus V's later restoration of the Temple to the Jews; and that the summarizer or Jason put them together out of order. The Roman envoys, Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, are otherwise unknown.

The numbers. The book's armies and casualties are large: 120,000 Galatians, when "the six thousand destroyed a hundred and twenty thousand" (8:20), though the verse has just said eight thousand Jews fought with four thousand Macedonians; Timothy with 120,000 foot (12:20); Lysias with 80,000 and 80 elephants (11:2–4), where 1 Maccabees has 60,000 foot and 5,000 horse; 110,000 foot and 300 scythed chariots (13:2); 35,000 of Nicanor's men killed (15:27). The New American Bible's introduction says plainly that the writer exaggerates the numbers. Here 1 Maccabees is usually preferred.

The shaping. The book is rhetorical, theological history of a kind Greek writers also produced, aimed at moving readers. Its writer says he leaves exactness to the historian (2:28). Its order serves its theology: Antiochus must die before the Temple is purified, so that the persecutor is punished and the sanctuary restored in the right sequence. Most historians treat its heavenly appearances as the writer's way of saying that God fought for Judas, and its speeches as composed.

The Catholic and Orthodox answer. The churches that read it as Scripture read it as true history in the form its writer chose. Catholic teaching on literary forms (Divino Afflante Spiritu; Dei Verbum 12) asks what the writer meant to assert, and the writer himself distinguishes between Jason's detail and his own summary (2:28–31). Bechtel defended the book's history point by point. The Orthodox churches have made no ruling on these questions known to us. A fair summary: trustworthy in its main events and its documents, the best source for the years before the revolt, freer than 1 Maccabees with order, numbers and the manner of Antiochus's death, and written to show God at work.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: the one God, Creator of all (7:23, 28; Genesis 1; Psalm 33:6–9); his care for his Temple and his people (3:39; 1 Kings 8:29); discipline that corrects and does not destroy (6:12–16; Deuteronomy 8:5; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11); the resurrection of the righteous (7:9, 14; Daniel 12:2; Isaiah 26:19; John 5:28–29); faithfulness to the Law even to death (6:18–31; Daniel 3; Daniel 6); angels who guard God's people (3:24–26; 15:23; 2 Kings 6:17; Psalm 34:7); God's judgment on the proud persecutor (9:5–12; Isaiah 14:12–15; Acts 12:23).
  • Goes beyond: (a) creation "not from things that were" (7:28; compare Hebrews 11:3; Romans 4:17), said more directly than anywhere in the Hebrew Bible and often read as creation from nothing, though whether it means that is asked on the chapter 7 page; (b) prayer and sacrifice for the dead (12:42–45), a practice the 66 books do not mention; (c) the dead praying for the living: Onias and Jeremiah in Judas's dream (15:12–14); (d) the martyrs' deaths turning God's anger from the nation (7:37–38), an idea close to Isaiah 53 and the New Testament's teaching on Christ's death; (e) new feasts, Hanukkah and Nicanor's Day (10:8; 15:36), added to the Law's feasts, as Purim was (Esther 9:20–32); (f) legends about Jeremiah and Nehemiah (1:18–2:15) not in their books.
  • Differs or may conflict: (a) Razis. The book praises a man who killed himself (14:37–46); the 66 books tell of suicides (Saul, Ahithophel, Zimri in 1 Kings 16:18, Judas) without praise, though Samson's death with the Philistines followed an answered prayer (Judges 16:28–30), and Hebrews 11:32 names him among the faithful; and "You must not murder" (Exodus 20:13) has been read by Jews and Christians as forbidding it. (b) An offering for the dead who sinned. Protestant readers see a conflict with Hebrews 9:27, which says that people die once and then face judgment, and with Christ's single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12–14); Catholic and Orthodox readers do not. (c) Nehemiah and the Temple. The second letter says Nehemiah "had built the temple and the altar" (1:18), but Ezra 3–6 says they were built under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, long before Nehemiah; Bechtel answered that Nehemiah completed the work, and one later manuscript (Codex 125, as Bechtel reports) reads "managed" instead of "built." (d) Jeremiah and the ark. 2:4–8 promises that the ark will be shown again; Jeremiah 3:16 says it will not be remembered or made again. The two can be read together, since Jeremiah speaks of a time when it will not be missed.
  • Each church's view: Catholic and Orthodox churches read 2 Maccabees as Scripture in harmony with the rest of their Old Testament and the New. Catholics read (b) of the second list as witness to prayer for the dead (Catechism 1032, which cites 12:45), and Catholic writers have long cited (c) for the saints' intercession; whether the saints in heaven pray for us is asked on the Revelation 5 page. The Orthodox also pray for the dead and ask the saints' prayers, and generally reject purgatory as the Latin church defined it. Both read Razis as a narrated deed, not a model (Augustine). Lutheran and Anglican churches read it as a human book, useful for the example of the martyrs, never to establish doctrine. Reformed, Baptist and most evangelical churches value its martyrs and its history, and see in (a) and (b) of the third list, and in its own epilogue, reasons why it is not inspired. The chapter pages give the readings on each passage.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you are Catholic or Orthodox (but not Ethiopian Orthodox), 2 Maccabees is in your Bible, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide to it. If you are Protestant, it is not Scripture for you, though Article VI commends such books for example of life, and Luther kept it for the sake of its martyrs. Either way, read it with respect and with an eye to the differences on this page.

how_to_read.h: Check which numbering your Bible uses
how_to_read.b: This site follows the Greek numbering of Swete and the King James Version. In the Vulgate, the Douay-Rheims and many Catholic Bibles the offering for the dead is 12:43–46 and the epilogue is 15:38–40. The Vulgate also differs in some readings (twelve thousand drachmas at 12:43).

how_to_read.h: Read it as a summary with a purpose
how_to_read.b: Start with the preface (2:19–32) and the epilogue (15:37–39). The writer tells you he is summarizing, that he wants to please and benefit you, and that he mixes plain history with what delights. Then read the story as Greek-speaking Jews would have: a moving history of God's care for his Temple and his people, with the feasts at the end of each half.

how_to_read.h: Read it beside 1 Maccabees and Daniel
how_to_read.b: Read 2 Maccabees 3–7 first, for the years before the revolt that only it tells, then 1 Maccabees 1–7 beside 2 Maccabees 8–15. Read Daniel 11:21–39 and Daniel 12:1–3 beside chapters 4–7: Daniel's "wise" who fall by sword and flame, and the sleepers who will awake, are given faces in Eleazar and the seven brothers. Note where the accounts differ, especially on the death of Antiochus.

how_to_read.h: Read the martyrs beside the New Testament
how_to_read.b: Read 6:18–7:42 and then Hebrews 11:32–40, Mark 12:18–27 and John 11:23–26. The New Testament's readers knew these stories. They explain why Jews of Jesus' day could believe in the resurrection, and why the church, from the start, honored those who died rather than deny God.

On prayer for the dead (12:43–45), the saints' prayers (15:12–14), Razis (14:37–46) and the writer's own apology (15:38), the churches give real answers, set out above and on the chapter pages; whether the saints in heaven pray for us is asked on the Revelation 5 page ("Do the saints in heaven pray for us, and may we ask them to?"). Read each in its strongest form before deciding.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "2 Maccabees, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants," and which numbering you use. It is the best source for the high priests' crisis before the revolt, the oldest story of the Maccabean martyrs, and a key text for the history of Jewish and Christian belief in the resurrection.
